lessons.title: 1 · Name the whole and its equal parts
lessons.goal: Describe a fraction as a number, identify its unit whole, and connect equal parts to distance from zero.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil; draw equal strips and mark a 0–1 number line. A helper may read or type your explanation. No tools, food or physical cutting are needed.
paragraphs:
START WITH A UNIT
Draw one strip. Call the entire strip one whole and label its ends 0 and 1. Divide it into four equal lengths. One length is one quarter, written 1/4. The denominator, 4, tells how many equal parts make this whole; the numerator, 1, counts how many of those parts we name.

WORKED EXAMPLE · COUNT DISTANCES, NOT TICK MARKS
Shade three of the four parts: 3/4. On the number line, start at 0 and travel three equal quarter-lengths: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4. Four intervals require five boundary marks including 0 and 1. Do not count the starting mark as a distance traveled. Four quarters reach 1; zero quarters stay at 0.

EQUAL IS ESSENTIAL
A strip split into one short piece and one long piece has two pieces, but they are not both halves. Fractions of a length use equal lengths. For a fraction of an area, use equal areas; pieces need not have the same shape. Always say what quantity is being divided.

SAME NUMBER, DIFFERENT PHYSICAL AMOUNT
One half is the number halfway from 0 to 1. Half of an 8 cm strip is 4 cm; half of a 12 cm strip is 6 cm. The fraction is the same, but the physical wholes differ. Equal-looking fraction diagrams support comparisons of amounts only when their wholes represent the same amount.

TRY THE FRACTION LAB
Open Fraction lab. Predict where A = 1/4 will end, then select it. Keep four equal parts and change the selected parts from 1 to 3. Describe what stays fixed and what moves. The lab explores numbers from 0 to 1; fractions above one and negative fractions are outside this introductory model.

EXPLAIN, THEN REVISIT
Use the new practice card. Draw a matching strip and number line for one answer. Later, choose a different denominator, mark every interval and explain why the final point is still 1. Numeric checks accept equivalent values; they do not judge the quality of your drawing.

PRACTICE CARD
PARTS CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[F1] One strip is one whole. It has six equal-length parts; five are shaded.
[F2] A 0–1 number line is divided into eight equal intervals. A point lies three intervals to the right of 0.
[F3] All six equal parts of the F1 strip are now shaded.
[F4] An 8 cm strip and a 12 cm strip each have half their length shaded.
[F5] Another strip is split into two unequal lengths.

hints: Count equal parts in the entire strip, including unshaded parts.
Use shaded parts over all equal parts: 5 over 6.
mistakes: The denominator names all six equal parts of the whole; it is not the shaded count.
One sixth is the unshaded part. The question asks for the shaded amount.

lessons.title: 2 · Rename and compare the same amount
lessons.goal: Build equivalent fractions by repartitioning, compare on the same whole, and challenge whole-number reasoning.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil; draw equal strips and mark a 0–1 number line. A helper may read or type your explanation. No tools, food or physical cutting are needed.
paragraphs:
KEEP THE AMOUNT; CHANGE THE PART SIZE
Shade two thirds of a strip. Split every third, shaded and unshaded, into two equal pieces. The whole now has six equal parts, of which four are shaded: 2/3 = 4/6. The endpoint did not move. Multiply both numerator and denominator by the same positive whole number to name finer equal pieces.

WORKED EXAMPLE · A COMMON UNIT
Compare 2/3 and 3/4 of the same whole. Split each third into four pieces and each quarter into three. Both strips now use twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Nine twelfths is greater than eight twelfths, so 3/4 is greater. The number-line endpoint for 3/4 is farther right.

WHY THE BIGGER DENOMINATOR CAN MEAN A SMALLER PIECE
With one whole fixed, six equal pieces are smaller than three equal pieces: 1/6 < 1/3. A denominator is not a score where bigger always means more. When numerators also change, neither denominator alone nor numerator alone settles the comparison.

REDUCE WITHOUT CHANGING THE ENDPOINT
Grouping the four shaded sixths into pairs gives two shaded thirds. Dividing numerator and denominator by the same common factor preserves the value: 4/6 = 2/3. Dividing only one number changes the amount. A numeric check here accepts either equivalent form; explain the regrouping yourself.

PREDICT IN THE LAB
Start A at 1/2 and B at 2/4. Change B to 3/6 by changing both controls. The endpoint should return to the same place. Then hold the numerator at one while changing the denominator. Predict each movement before changing a control, and use the displayed common pieces to explain it.

TRY, EXPLAIN, REVISIT
Use a fresh equal-parts drawing for the card. After practice, make your own unequal-denominator pair between zero and one. Compare it on a common unit and test whether reversing the order reverses the comparison.

PRACTICE CARD
EQUIVALENCE CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE

[E2] Compare 5/6 and 7/12 of the same unit whole.
[E3] The fraction 6/8 is to be renamed in quarters.
[E4] Compare one fifth and one third of the same whole.

lessons.title: 3 · Add and subtract equal-sized parts
lessons.goal: Use a common fraction unit to add or subtract, estimate the result, and explain why denominators are not added.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil; draw equal strips and mark a 0–1 number line. A helper may read or type your explanation. No tools, food or physical cutting are needed.
paragraphs:
COUNT THE SAME KIND OF PIECE
Two eighths plus three eighths make five eighths: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. The pieces are still eighths. Adding denominators would rename their size and would not describe the combined length.

WORKED EXAMPLE · RENAME BEFORE ADDING
To combine 1/4 and 1/2 of the same unit length, rename the half as two quarters. Now 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. Think of traveling one quarter from zero and then two more quarters. The original whole remains the unit; laying pieces together does not redefine it.

WORKED EXAMPLE · FIND THE GAP
Subtract the half again: 3/4 − 1/2 = 3/4 − 2/4 = 1/4. On a number line, the distance from 1/2 to 3/4 is 1/4. Check by addition: 1/4 + 1/2 returns 3/4. Add and subtract the counts only after their piece sizes match.

ESTIMATE BEFORE CALCULATING
A positive amount added to 1/2 must give more than 1/2. Subtracting a positive amount must give less than the starting amount. If a result violates that check, inspect the fraction units. These practice sums stay between zero and one; the same equal-unit reasoning also extends beyond one.

COMPARE BEFORE COMBINING
Use Fraction lab to see that 1/2 and 2/4 end at the same point. The lab compares two amounts; it does not add its strips. Use paper to place the fractional lengths end to end, or follow the worked diagram steps, to model addition.

TRY, EXPLAIN, REVISIT
For each practice sum, state a common denominator, rename both fractions, calculate and check the size of the answer. A least common denominator is convenient but another common multiple also works. Later, check a subtraction by reversing it with addition.

PRACTICE CARD
COMBINING CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[C1] Combine 1/3 and 1/6 of one unit strip.
[C2] Find the gap from 1/4 to 5/8 on the same 0–1 line.
[C3] Add 2/5 and 1/10 of the same whole.
[C4] Someone writes 1/3 + 1/6 = 2/9 by adding both top numbers and both bottom numbers.

lessons.title: 4 · Find a fraction of a stated quantity
lessons.goal: Find a unit fraction, scale to several shares, recover a whole from one share, and keep the answer's unit.
lessons.materials: Paper and pencil; draw equal strips and mark a 0–1 number line. A helper may read or type your explanation. No tools, food or physical cutting are needed.
paragraphs:
WHAT DOES 'OF' REFER TO?
In '3/4 of 20 cards', the whole collection contains 20 cards. Split the collection into four equal groups: each has 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cards. Three groups contain 3 × 5 = 15 cards. The fraction is 3/4; the requested count is 15 cards. Do not report 3/4 cards as the count.

WORKED EXAMPLE · SHARE FIRST, THEN SCALE
Find 3/5 of 30 cards. One fifth of the collection is 30 ÷ 5 = 6 cards; three fifths is 3 × 6 = 18 cards. The strip diagram represents the whole collection by one unit strip. Each fifth means six cards, not one card. The two unselected fifths contain 12 cards, so 18 + 12 checks the original 30.

WORK BACK TO THE WHOLE
If one fifth is six cards, five such groups contain 30 cards. If two fifths is twelve cards, first find one fifth: 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Then multiply by five. State what fraction the given number represents before multiplying or dividing.

SIZE AND UNITS CHECK
For a positive whole, taking a fraction strictly between zero and one gives less than the whole. Taking zero gives none, and taking one gives the entire amount. Fractions of lengths may be non-whole numbers of centimetres. A task involving indivisible objects may need a different interpretation when equal sharing is impossible; the card counts here share exactly.

USE THE REPRESENTATION CAREFULLY
In Fraction lab, A = 3/5 locates a fraction of one unit. To interpret it as cards, separately state what the whole is worth. Changing a whole from 30 cards to 50 cards leaves the fraction's point fixed but changes three fifths from 18 cards to 30 cards.

TRY, EXPLAIN, TRANSFER
After the card, invent a whole count divisible by six and find five sixths of it. Explain a unit share, the selected shares, the remaining share and a total check. Return to Measure & plan to connect fractions to physical lengths and drawing dimensions.

PRACTICE CARD
QUANTITY CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[Q1] A collection has 28 cards. Find 3/4 of the collection.
[Q2] A paper line is 18 cm long. Find 2/3 of its length.
[Q3] One fifth of another collection is 7 cards. Find the whole collection.
[Q4] Another collection has 24 cards. Someone claims 3/8 of it is 64 cards after calculating 24 ÷ 3 × 8.

questions.prompt: How many cards are 3/4 of the collection in Q1?
questions.explanation: One quarter is 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cards. Three quarters is 3 × 7 = 21 cards. The remaining seven bring the total back to 28.
hints: First find how many cards are in one of four equal groups.
Multiply seven cards per quarter by three quarters.
mistakes: Seven is one quarter. The question asks for three quarters.
Three quarters names the fraction; the answer needs the number of cards.

questions.explanation: One third of 18 cm is 6 cm. Two thirds is 12 cm, leaving 6 cm. Together they recover the full 18 cm.
hints: Divide the 18 cm whole into three equal lengths.
Take two lengths of 6 cm each.
mistakes: Six centimetres is one third, not two thirds.
Dividing by two then multiplying by three reverses the roles. Two thirds of a positive length must be smaller than the whole.

QUANTITY CARD — ORIGINAL PAPER PRACTICE
[Q1] A collection has 28 cards. Find 3/4 of the collection.
[Q2] A paper line is 18 cm long. Find 2/3 of its length.
[Q3] One fifth of another collection is 7 cards. Find the whole collection.
[Q4] Another collection has 24 cards. Someone claims 3/8 of it is 64 cards after calculating 24 ÷ 3 × 8.

questions.prompt: How many cards are in the whole collection in Q3?
questions.explanation: Seven cards is one fifth. The whole has five such equal groups: 5 × 7 = 35 cards. Checking one fifth of 35 returns seven.
hints: The seven cards are a share, not the entire collection.
How many one-fifth shares make the whole?
mistakes: Dividing seven by five treats it as the whole. Seven is already one fifth.
Add five equal groups of seven, not the numbers five and seven.

questions.prompt: Which critique correctly addresses Q4?
choices: A
64 must be right because the calculation used both 3 and 8.
B
The result must be below 24; one eighth is 3 cards, so three eighths is 9 cards.
C
3/8 always means three cards, regardless of the collection size.
questions.explanation: Split 24 into eight equal groups to get three cards per group, then take three groups to get nine. The estimate below 24 rejects 64 before exact calculation.
hints: Is three eighths less than one whole?
Divide by the number of equal shares, then take three shares.
mistakes: A
Using the numbers is not enough: the denominator sets eight equal groups and the numerator selects three.
C
The numerator counts shares, not individual cards. Each share contains three cards here.

questions.prompt: Invent a collection divisible by six. Find five sixths, show a unit-share calculation, and verify with the remaining sixth.
questions.explanation: Compare for: a positive whole count divisible by six, equal one-sixth groups, five selected shares and one remaining share that together recover the whole. Example: 'For 42 cards, each sixth is 7; five sixths is 35; the remaining 7 gives 35 + 7 = 42.' Other valid counts and explanations are welcome.
hints: Choose a multiple of six, such as six equal groups of a count you know.
Check that five groups plus one group recover the starting collection.

diagram.description: Every full strip represents the same unit whole. Equal cells show the denominator; shaded cells show the numerator. The point below each strip locates that fraction on a 0–1 number line. All steps appear in the worksheet.

steps.title: One whole means 30 cards
steps.caption: The entire unit strip stands for 30 cards divided into five equal groups.

steps.title: Find one fifth
steps.caption: One fifth is one of five equal groups: 30 divided by 5 gives 6 cards.

steps.title: Take three fifths
steps.caption: Three selected groups contain 18 cards; the other two contain 12. Their total is 30 cards.
